utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I notice the absence amongst the accused of Beara and Popovic. Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I was just informed this morning that Mr. Popovic is sick and he signed a waiver not to be present this morning, today, at this trial. And you have my consent also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. And Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Beara is also ill but I believe he will be here tomorrow morning and I believe he's also signed a waiver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We got yesterday's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yesterday's, yes. I asked him to be sure to sign one for today's sitting as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you waive as well, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, for today's sitting, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: From the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Bourgon and the absence of Ms. Condon, absence of Mr. Ostojic and that's about it. Prosecution, it's Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Vanderpuye. At present, the witness is already in his chair. I think we can -- unless there are preliminary matters that you would like to raise, we can proceed with his testimony. Go ahead, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and good morning to you, good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dragutinovic. Mr. Dragutinovic, I just wanted to clarify something that I read in the record just yesterday and it relates to your testimony which appears on page 12569 through page 12570 of the transcript and that was in relation to the question of to whom the commander of the military police reported to. I just wanted to clarify this issue. Did you mean to suggest that the commander of the military police reported to the chief of security -- to the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military police unit is a unit affiliated with the staff and it had its commander. Following that logic he should have reported to the Chief of Staff himself, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And are you sure that those were the rules in effect in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've explained that because of the efficiency of command and more effective control, we curtailed the procedure at that time so that the commander of the military police could have reported to, and did indeed report to, the chief of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did the commander of the military police unit also report to the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the military police unit did not report to the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think we left off yesterday, and you had indicated that -- I think you just reached the point where you had stopped on the night of the 14th. At the point that you stopped, did you receive any further orders?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 14th, in the evening, we didn't, because our previous task was clear, and in a certain way we had reached the positions that were part of the original task, and we were preparing our units to continue operating on the following day without any special orders because we complied with the previous orders in doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: On the 15th, in the morning, can you tell us what happened?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that morning, we should have proceeded our operations leading towards the village of Bortici [phoen] and further on towards Zepa. However, the commander ordered us not to move the units until he came back from the forward command post of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The commander of your unit, you mean Commander Pandurevic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm referring to Commander Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the forward command post of the corps, you mean the Drina Corps; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Drina Corps forward command post in the village of Krivaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Around what time did the commander leave that morning?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning, around 8.00 or thereabouts. I'm not sure but it was in the morning. The units had already been ready, the operations could have started already, even before he left, but we put everything on hold because the commander had left and we were waiting for his return.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you know who he went to go see at the forward command post in Krivaca?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I only know that he went to the forward command post. There, there was the operations commander, Mr. Krstic, with several other officers. I don't know who these officers were. So he did not have any special appointments with anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Around what time did he get back?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have been between 8.00 and 9.00, but let's say it was around 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what did he tell you about his appointment or his meeting at the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the commander returned, my first impression was that he was rather angry. It was immediately clear to me that something had happened or that something was happening. I asked him what this was all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what did he say?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a nutshell he told me this - I don't know whether I'll be able to quote him, but he said: The 28th Division is already behind our brigade, the Zvornik Brigade. It's threatened in Memici, Baljkovica, Petkovica [as interpreted]. In other words he said, "The things that I had warned them about did happen the way I had envisaged."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did he come back with any instructions with respect to your unit?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just add to this that my first reaction to that was to ask, "What about the town of Zvornik?" And then the reply was that everything there was okay. The next instruction was to prepare the units to pull out from the positions that they had reached, to prepare them for march and in the shortest possible time that we should start moving towards Zvornik, only the Tactical Group 1 under the command of Mr. Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did he tell you where he received the information, or from whom he'd received the information rather, concerning the situation that he was telling you about?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Commander Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what happened after you had this conversation with Commander Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We pulled the units from the lines reached and we got ready for return to Zvornik. The commander waited a certain while to be abreast of the situation, to see whether the column was being formed properly, and then he headed for Zvornik himself. He immediately told me that the mechanised unit should be at the rear, that I should be with that unit, and that the axis should be the same for us and that when we reached Zvornik we should go to Caparde and Memici, in other words to head towards the defence sector of the 7th Battalion. In other words he already provided me with some guidelines as to what to do with that armoured -- mixed armoured and mechanised unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. So he provided you with these instructions while you were still in the area of Pozeplje?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And around what time -- what time did the commander leave for Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 10.00. I'm not sure. But it couldn't have been after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And around what time did he arrive, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It took him at least two hours to travel the distance. I don't know when he arrived at the command of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What time did you leave?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My unit departed after 10.00, when all the units were already ready and on their way to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What time did you arrive?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived in Zvornik between 1400 and 1315 hours. I arrived in the neighbourhood Zlatne Vode.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What happened after you arrived?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed in that neighbourhood. An officer from the command arrived there, Major Mihajlo Galic is his name. And he brought us an order which said that we should take the Snagovo-Caparde route to arrive in the defence sector of the 7th Battalion but that I should wait until the fuel arrived for the combat vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you ever -- well, did you proceed to Caparde at some point?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we got fuel, I departed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did Major Galic tell you where the order came from that he was transmitting?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Commander Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And at that point, did you know where Commander Pandurevic was?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only knew that he was somewhere in the defence area of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. When you reached Caparde, did you receive any other orders?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was clear from the previous order why I was there. I was supposed to support the 7th Battalion, i.e., to control the road and that area around Memici, Caparde and Crni Vrh. The last location was very important for the Zvornik Brigade at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you have any further contact or communications with your commander, Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could have only contacted him through the 7th Battalion, and I indeed established that contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And when was that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived at the 7th Battalion, which was some time in the afternoon, on that day, on the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is that where your unit remained following your arrival?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They remained there. I received an order to return a tank and an APC to the Parlog sector, i.e., in the defence sector of the 6th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were you engaged in any combat operations that day?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I arrived in the area of the 7th Battalion, there were attacks from the front line with a view to taking the Pandurica feature which was very important in the whole picture. I realised that my commander had dispatched my unit for that very reason because if the enemy had taken over the Pandurica facility, as well as Tisova Kosa, Cetino Brdo and Crni Vrh, the Zvornik Brigade would have been put under a lot of pressure and into a very unfavourable position.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We direct your attention to the 16th of July. Were you engaged in any combat operations on that day?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning of the 16th, the 7th Battalion also came under attack. The attack was repelled. And we could also hear the sounds of battle in the area of the 4th Battalion. That was in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was your unit involved in any specific combat operations on that day?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The unit was just support, only if the battalion commander asked for the unit to open fire on certain targets, then the unit would become active, actively engaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what were the specific actions of your unit that day?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 16th, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: On the 16th, yes.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To provide support to the units of the 7th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were you in contact with your commander on that day?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Again, through the command of the 7th Battalion, i.e., through the commander of the 7th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you tell us about the night of the 16th?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my contacts with the commander and the commander of the 7th Battalion, I learned that negotiations were going on and an agreement had been reached on letting through the 28th Division and the civilian population that was in the back of that 28th Division, through a passage that the 4th Battalion had created and that by the 17th there should be a corridor open to let these people through to the territory under the control of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Can I take you into the 17th of July? On that day, did you have any contact with Commander Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made a contact with the commander through my assistant, Ljubo Bojanovic, who had arrived in the defence centre of the 7th Battalion with a company from the 16th Motorised Brigade of the 1st Krajina Corps, which had been dispatched in another direction, but it was diverted in our direction in order to assist us in all the actions that we were engaged in.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you receive any new orders on the 17th with respect to your unit?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order was to attach a squad from the 7th Battalion to this company, to put it on the strength of that company, that we carry out reconnaissance and come to the back of the 4th Battalion to check whether there are any BiH troops there and to simply reconnoitre the situation in that sector. The goal was to see whether the agreements that had been reached on the following day were being honoured.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And did you -- do you have any idea where your commander was at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander was at the forward command post. I knew that. I knew that from my assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And just for the record, where is that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forward command post was in the area of Delici village, near Kitovnice village, which was in the area of defence of the 6th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you receive any orders with respect to the corridor itself, whether or not your unit -- well, just did you receive any orders with respect to the corridor itself?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My orders were to check whether that piece of area, piece of territory that was agreed, that breach through which the forces of the 28th Division and the civilian population was free to be occupied by the 28th Division, whether they had already entered there or whether they had already moved perhaps outside the agreed area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did your unit participate in the closure of the corridor on that day?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that day, the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let's go into the 18th. Can you tell us when the next time it was that you actually saw your commander, Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him in the afternoon, after accomplishing the tasks that I had received for the 17th and the 18th, and after that I returned to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And specifically what did your unit engage in with respect to the corridor on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Following the orders issued by the commander on the 17th, that were messengered to me, and in view of the fact that a platoon from the Podrinje Detachment arrived in the area, upon direct orders of the commander, with a task to return to the defence area of the 7th Battalion, and use that company to strengthen the defence area of the 7th Battalion, just to prevent the possibility that some new forces from the front might take advantage of this, we had to strengthen that area of the defence and we did that with the forces of the 7th Battalion on the 17th, whereas on the 18th, together with the commanders of the 4th and the 7th Battalion, I was occupying positions in the area from which the 4th Battalion had moved earlier, so that basically the 4th Battalion just recovered its basic positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And on the 17th, did you see anybody from the superior command in your vicinity?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was only me, my assistant and the commander's company that were there, and the commander of that platoon from the Podrinje Detachment, which had arrived from the area of Delici village.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Are you familiar with a person with the last name of Trkulja?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I asked that commander, the commander of that unit, I asked him what was going on at the forward command post in view of the orders I had received. He just said vaguely that there had been an officer there from the superior command but he was a simple soldier who didn't know much. I learned it only later when I returned to the command, I learned that from the operations duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when was that? Was that on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should have been on the 17th that that officer from the superior command was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No. I'm sorry, when is it that you learned why that officer was there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I met up with that unit from the Podrinje Detachment in the same area where I was with the 4th Battalion. I'm not sure exactly when, in what time interval, that officer had been there on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what did you learn?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, I learned that he was in fact an officer from the superior command who had visited the forward command post, sized up the situation in the brigade, and wanted to know about developments of the past days, probably in order to be able to inform the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, could you tell us what superior command this officer was from?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you that because I'm not sure. I know I didn't know Mr. Trkulja except by name so if I said he was from the corps or from the Main Staff, I could be mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, on the 19th, can you tell us what happened?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 19th, I was already at the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And did you have a meeting on the 19th at the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by the operation of the brigade and that was regular procedure, there was a briefing every day with the commander in the presence of his Chief of Staff and his operations assistant which was myself. I always participated in that briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And what was discussed at this particular briefing?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, the main topic were the problems and developments of the 15th, 16th, 17th and the 18th, and the main topic was the consolidation of that 4th Battalion, which had suffered the greatest impact in its area and, of course, we had to organise replenishment with materiel and equipment, to organise a new command post, to provide adequate communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you discuss at this briefing the issue of the corridor and whether Mr. Trkulja, as you put it, was there under those circumstances and with regard to the opening of that corridor on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. We did not. Mr. Trkulja was there. He picked up the information that he needed, and he returned to the command to which he was sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. So that was never discussed?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Your brigade commander was at that meeting on the 19th; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the commander was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was the Chief of Staff there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff was there. All of us who normally attended the briefings.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And from that day forward, was your commander regularly at the command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was regularly at the command all the way up to the 31st July and the 1st of August, when I was together with the commander in the area of Zepa. Before that, we were at the command, and in the defence area of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Just bear with me for one moment, Mr. Dragutinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just want to clarify something, and it is actually your last answer. Is it your recollection that on the 31st of July and the 1st of August, that you were in the area of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You sure about that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't get that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you sure about that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Dragutinovic. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you clarify with the witness, at one time the witness referred to Mr. Trkulja as a simple soldier and another time he referred to him as an officer from superior command. So whether he knew any ranks or --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Kwon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think earlier in your testimony, Mr. Dragutinovic, you mentioned a simple soldier in the same breath, as it were, as Mr. Trkulja. Do you know, first of all, what the rank of Mr. Trkulja was?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what was that rank?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must be a misunderstanding. The presence of Mr. Trkulja was notified to me by the platoon commander who was a simple soldier, so he couldn't have known Mr. Trkulja as an officer and he wasn't able to tell me who that officer was. So I didn't say that Trkulja was a simple soldier. I said a simple soldier told me that a senior officer was at the forward command post, but he, as a simple soldier, was not able to identify him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So is this Mr. Trkulja, Nedjeljko Trkulja, who was a colonel?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The question is whether or not the Mr. Trkulja you're referring to is Nedjeljko Trkulja and whether or not he was a colonel. Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably he couldn't have been less than lieutenant-colonel. He could have been only higher than lieutenant-colonel. Colonel, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dragutinovic. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a hint that it's Mr. Haynes who is going to start because I saw you preparing yourself. How much -- how long do you expect to cross-examine this witness? You had asked for four hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I hope to finish today but we'll -- let's see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dragutinovic.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some questions for probably the rest of the day on behalf of your commander, Vinko Pandurevic. And I want to start really by just clarifying your role as the duty operations officer -- I'm sorry, not the duty operations officer but as the operations officer. It's right, isn't it, that in your capacity as operations officer, you would receive tasks together with the Chief of Staff directly from the commander?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You were not, within the structure of the brigade, an assistant to the commander yourself, but you were responsible for receiving and carrying out orders?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was assistant Chief of Staff, but in that position, upon the commander's request, I would attend all important briefings and I could receive orders directly from the commander without going through the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to see if you agree with something somebody else said in this case which is that the operations officer is the soul of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could put it that way because the operations officer has available to him all written, printed and other documents and participates in the elaboration of all documents, both combat and non-combat, and participates in all the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Would you also agree that the operations officer was more instrumental in the work of the command than, for example, the assistant to the commander for logistics or the assistant to the commander for moral, religious and legal affairs?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in view of my responsibilities and all the assignments I had, I don't think that anything in the command is less important than another thing, but in my section, the one I led, we were abreast of all the latest developments in the brigade, which is not necessarily the case with the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And is it also right that other assistants to the commander would often come directly to you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was -- he would.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You've probably already said this but just to confirm, you were always present at morning briefings; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always attended morning briefings and when assistants could not resolve some problems without the commander or the Chief of Staff, who were for some reason absent, they would address me with their problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you had access to all documentation necessary for brigade combat operations: Orders, decisions, working maps, military reports, plans and the like?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the normal procedure of command, the commander commands all units and all his ideas were elaborated through the Chief of Staff and the operations officer. So I was aware of all the documents prepared at the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And lastly this about your particular role: Part of your responsibilities included checking, together with other assistants to the commander, the operations of the subordinate units of the brigade, especially the battalions?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I often went to inspect the work of battalion commands and I also had to monitor the degree of execution of tasks that the commander would assign to all units, and then report to the commander. In addition to the fact that battalion commanders were, of course, duty-bound to report to the commander on the execution of their own assignments but somehow it still went mostly through me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to move on now to ask you a few questions about the staff generally and your boss, the Chief of Staff. It's right, isn't it, that within the brigade, the staff is the most populous department, in other words, it has the most people working within it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And if one wanted to characterise the respective roles of the commander and the Chief of Staff, it would be that the commander is a sort of general manager and the Chief of Staff a technical manager?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The staff is an executive organ of the command and it's headed by the Chief of Staff. So anything that the commander conceived or ordered is monitored by the Chief of Staff and the Chief of Staff issues commands in the course of combat operations. So the commander is like a general manager, and the rest of us executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. You'd agree, wouldn't you, the staff had the most important tasks in the brigade and that all the information in the brigade was gathered there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that the Chief of Staff was familiar with all the other organs of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The other organs of the brigade were not subordinate to the Chief of Staff but he could not function in relation to the staff unless he had all the information from the other organs, that's correct, too, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. In order to be able to function, the command had to ensure that the Chief of Staff was informed of everything, of all the operations, activities, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, the Chief of Staff had the right to give orders to subordinate units of the brigade as well, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: He did not, as Chief of Staff, have the right of command, but he could give orders or tasks according to the order of the commander?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could also command, but only in keeping with the tasks already issued by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you for correcting me. Perhaps we could illustrate this by an example. If, for example, the brigade received an order to attack a certain position --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: -- the commander, the Chief of Staff, the operational organs and the other organs, would conceive a plan and on the basis of their suggestions, the commander would form a general idea which would form an order; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff would prepare a proposal or an outline plan and the commander would either accept that, reject it or amend it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The final decision would be written down on paper, which would contain defined, concrete tasks for the units, and the Chief of Staff would give the tasks to the subordinate units that he controlled and order them to do their work?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, that's how the Chief of Staff would operate generally when he was Chief of Staff, but the Chief of Staff was also the deputy commander of the brigade, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of his position, the Chief of Staff was also an assistant so the brigade commander had to have a deputy for situations when he is not able to command for some reason. Then the Chief of Staff would take over automatically and in some cases a special order would be issued to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come on to that but when the commander was absent, the Chief of Staff had full authority, that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He takes over the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: He does not act according to the command of the commander; he is only subordinate, during that period, to higher command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he commands the brigade, he is subordinate to the superior command, but when commander is still around and he's just not able to deal with command temporarily, then not. When the Chief of Staff is, however, temporarily appointed by the superior command, then he reports exclusively to the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, we'll come on in due course to analyse in more detail two periods when Vinko Pandurevic was away from the brigade command. The first of those was between the 4th and the 15th of July, when he was in Srebrenica and Zepa. You remember that because you were there with him, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the second period we will come to look at is between the 7th of August and the 16th of September when he was commanding the Drinski Brigade in Krajina, and you were there with him as well, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, the first of those periods is a period of 11 days and the second is a period of I think something like 45 days. But in terms of the authority available to Dragan Obrenovic whilst his commander was away, there is no practical difference between those two periods, is there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was appointed to be commander then and he completely took over command of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just in terms of when an order was required, the commander and the Chief of Staff were on slightly different pay scales, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'll ask this question. It may be that you don't know the answer to this as well. But if the commander was away for a period of more than a month, an order was required from corps command for ordinary fiscal purposes, just so the Chief of Staff got paid more. That's the only reason an order was required for a period of more than a month, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to answer your question. The main reason for the appointment was the fact that somebody had to be in command over the unit, over such a long period of time, and that's when a commander is appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dragutinovic. I'm going to move on from that now, just to clear up a few things yesterday that you said about the structure of the Zvornik Brigade. When you were answering questions to Mr. Vanderpuye, you identified that the staff had several operative organs. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The staff had only one operative organ, and this was the organ headed by myself. Please be more specific and then I'll be able to answer. What are you referring to actually?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. It's my mistake, not yours. I shouldn't have used the word "operative". The staff had several organs which had links with separate units within the battalion, that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: For example, as you told us yesterday, there was a direct link between the chief of engineering within the staff and the engineering company within the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And similarly, there is a direct link between the chief of signals within the staff and the signals unit within the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just to carry on a little further but not exhaustively, a direct link between the staff artillery organ and the mixed artillery unit?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the mixed artillery division because the chief of artillery was also the commander of the mixed artillery division.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And those links within an ordinary brigade structure provide a formal relation -- a functional relationship between the organ of the staff and the unit within the brigade, don't they?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To provide for the efficiency of command and a more effective use of those units. That was the only reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But within the Zvornik Brigade, those functional relationships were, in fact, command relationships, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Because Commander Pandurevic authorised the chief of the signals organ to command the signals company and the chief of the engineering organ to command the engineering company, for example?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If there was no written order, that was the customary way we functioned, and the underlying reason was the efficient command and use of these units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And so, further to what you were telling us earlier, the Chief of Staff was directly responsible for signals, engineering and artillery units, that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I have to expand on that. The staff had its units, the signals unit, the engineers unit, the military police unit. These units were affiliated with the staff, and there was also the logistics battalion. Those were not units that would be at the level of battalion, whereas the mixed artillery division was a separate unit and it was separate from the staff, from the command of the staff. In other words, it was not affiliated with the staff as the others that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you but you've also reminded me of something else I should have put to you and that is that within the Zvornik Brigade, the assistant to the commander for logistics was authorised to command the rear battalion as well, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The assistant commander for logistics was directly subordinated to the commander, and it was part of his activity to look after the, and be responsible for, the rear battalion which was directly subordinated to the command of the assistant commander for the rear, and again for the reasons of functionality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, given everything you said to us yesterday and the clarifications you've just given today, I wonder whether you'd mind now just looking at a diagram for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And could we put into e-court 7D622.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, take your time to familiarise yourself with the document, Mr. Dragutinovic, and apologies for the way it's set out. It was just the best way to fit it on to one page. But on the left-hand side of the document, you can see the various organ -- the staff and its various organs?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And as far as you were aware, are all the organs of the staff of the Zvornik Brigade there listed?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that they are all there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you can see that there are a series of red or pinkish red lines emanating from the commander to the assistants to the command and the Chief of Staff and down to the battalions and the subordinate units of the brigade, indicating his command over those units. And you'd agree with that, would you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to this scheme, the commander commands all units, and this is the brigade structure which doesn't differ much from what was shown to me by the Prosecutor. This is only a different way of representing the same thing. The structure is the same but the schematic differs a little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, what's the origin of this document? Is it one prepared by the Defence or is it one supplied by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's one we've prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One you prepared. Okay. Could you also maybe -- I don't want to anticipate your -- any of your questions but I think it would help us follow better if he would indicate in which box he would fit himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You can even put a mark on it and put your initials by it, but would you please indicate which role you fulfilled within the staff of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm marking this square here, the organ for operative and training tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, could you as neatly as you can, put MD within that square?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I take it it's the upper of the two boxes because he's put the MD --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the upper box.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. It is where we have, "Organ za ONP", just for clarity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, organ for training and operative tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. And thank you, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dragutinovic, all really I want to make sure we agree about is that we can see emanating from some of the organs of the staff down to some of the subordinate units of the brigade some dotted lines. Can you see those?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And they are intended to indicate the functional relationships that you've talked about between the organs of the staff and their associated subordinate units within the brigade, and would you agree that they do accurately reflect --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Does that mean you do agree with me that they accurately reflect those functional relationships between those organs and units?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the exact relationship but let's take, for example, the signals organ, with the chief, and you have the dotted line connecting it to the signals company, i.e., there is a direct link with the staff affiliated unit. Or, for example, any other. The artillery organ is linked with the mixed artillery division, i.e., the chief of artillery according to this schematic is linked to the mixed artillery division.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now just briefly --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that applies to all of the other such units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dragutinovic. Now, just moving away from the staff, across to the right, we can see the organ for logistics headed by Sreten Milosevic. Can you see that, contained within a brown hatched box?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And from that organ, we can see a dotted line coming down to the rear battalion. Does that correctly reflect another functional relationship within the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it here, yes. That's how the brigade functioned, from Sreten Milosevic to the rear battalion, all to provide for easier command and use of all these organs, units and staff affiliated organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Dragutinovic. I'm afraid I have to ask you to sign this in the bottom, probably left-hand corner is the clearest area, so can you put MD again in the bottom left-hand corner and put today's date on it which I think is the 14th of June.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And can that document now be preserved and saved? I can't see a date on it. I don't know if the witness has put one on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. It's on the right-hand margin bottom and so that would fit in even though it's not on the part where there is the script. So you don't need to worry about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, can we move on, please? You've told us that another part of your function was, at least in part, the administrative work of the Zvornik Brigade. And I want you to tell us now a little bit about the duties of the duty operations officer within the command of the brigade. Briefly, could you state what the duties of the duty operations officer were within the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty operations officer was in charge of all the documents that were handled by the brigade. There was a staff office in which all data were processed. Whatever came in writing to the brigade, all that could be found in the staff office. The duty operations were organised in the units starting with the brigade level upwards. It was a daily obligation that lasted around the clock. The duty operations officer had his assistant, and the duty operations officer in the brigade had to be a higher ranking officer, and his assistant could have a lower rank and a somewhat lower position than the operations officer himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And is it right that within the brigade, a roster was kept of officers who were supposed to do duty operations duties?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operations department published a roster seven days in advance for the duties of the duty operations officer and his assistant. And this could also be found in the office of the operations department. So it was well known in advance who would be taking the duty and on what days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. It's right, isn't it, that the responsibility for the creation of a roster of duty officers and the command of the duty officers was provided for by the rules of the JNA, the work of the command and staff?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. By and large these provisions were adopted from the former rules of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just so we can have a look at the various sources of that, can we have a look, please, at P699, page 34 in the English and page 36 in the B/C/S? And can we scroll down so the witness can have a look at point 65? Mr. Dragutinovic, are you able to read point 65? Is it clear enough for you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll do my best, although -- okay then. 65? "The duty operative officer and his assistant are command officers that are determined according to a roster. If a duty shift is being established, then the duty officer and his assistant are part of that shift. The operative duty at the command post is organised by the Chief of Staff or the deputy commander and at the PKM," which should be IKM, I suppose, "it is done at the assistant -- by the assistant commander for logistics. At other command posts, the duty operations are organised by the most senior officer. The operative duty officers' subordinates are all organs of internal service at the command post." And this is how the operative duty functioned in our brigade as well. I would add to this that the duty operations officer in practical terms, during his duty, had to be well abreast of all important events that had taken place on that day in the brigade, in the subordinate units. He had to monitor the compliance with certain tasks. He had to inform the command thereof, to convey orders and at certain moments, when he could not convey certain orders of the superior -- to either the commander or his deputy, he assumed the responsibility for the performance of such tasks upon himself or better said, in our brigade, a duty operations officer was not merely a courier who conveyed messages or transmitted orders. He was more than that. He was a direct participant in all the events that had a bearing on the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And was it the position in accordance with those rules in the Zvornik Brigade that the roster was the responsibility of the Chief of Staff and that the duty operations officer was subordinate to the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the case pursuant to the rules. The operatives in my department were in charge of that roster. The Chief of Staff would issue orders and pursuant to those orders we would make the roster that had to be strictly complied with. The commander did not influence the roster as such. He did not interfere with our proposal for the roster.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And I just briefly want to go through with you some of the documents that were kept at the command by the duty operations officer. Firstly, he kept a notebook, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The duty operations officer kept a notebook in which he recorded all information that he received from the superior command, parts of the brigades, the subordinate units, the Chief of Staff, the commanders. He recorded everything that came to him. Everything was recorded in that notebook. Some information was recorded only briefly, in short outlines, and some was recorded in an extended version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the information in the notebook could contain personal messages, messages for people within the brigade and the like? It was quite literally a notebook, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a notebook, which contained all sorts of information, even personal information sent to an officer in the command or even to the soldiers on the strength of the brigade units, and this was all recorded. Nothing could be omitted, deleted. Nothing could be tampered with. It was a very colourful notebook that was a true reflection of what was happening on the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. There were two other books kept within the brigade that recorded daily events. The second one was the duty officer's diary or logbook, as we call it in this case. That was a document which derived substantially from the contents of the notebook, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The diary was based on the information in the notebook, with the caveat that personal information and things that were not connected with the function of the brigade and its units were omitted. All the important orders from the superior command, the information from the battalions, the orders of the commander of the brigade, the information from other subordinate units, were entered in the duty operations officer's logbook.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how often would the logbook be written up?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The logbook had to be kept every day, after the duty period expired because the logbook had to be brought to the morning briefings when the duty operations officer informed the commander of the events that the commander could not attend or wasn't privy to. The logbook was part of that briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thirdly, there was a document called the war diary, which I think was written up every few days. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The war diary should have been a document that contained the most important information relative to the function of the brigade, the war operations and other tasks. It wasn't kept every day. Sometimes it was kept retroactively. The war diary was kept in the operations department. It sometimes happened though that the operations department did not have anybody to man it for a day or two. That's why the information was collected from the operations logbook and the documents that had arrived, and then the entries would be made into the war diary on a certain day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's very helpful. And one last question before I think you're entitled to a break. It's right also that there was a duty officers' notebook kept at the barracks as well?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All documents were kept at the barracks. They were not allowed to be taken out of the barracks. They were not even allowed to be taken out of the designated rooms. If you are talking about the duty operations logbook, it had to be in his room. The war diary was at the operations section.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just to be clear, Mr. Dragutinovic, I'm talking about a separate notebook which was the barracks duty officer's notebook.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In that case, I'm mistaken. If you meant the duty officer at the barracks, he didn't work all the time. That institution was introduced in 1995 and the idea was to establish some order in the barracks so that the duty operations officer would have some insight into the functioning of the brigade, and that book was kept by the duty officer at the barracks. The duty officer would bring that book to the operations officer to sign after reviewing it, and after that, it went to the duty officer at the barracks. And I have to emphasise the duty officer at the barracks would be appointed or relieved by the duty operations officer. It was not up to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I think that's probably time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Dragutinovic, if you don't mind, can we just summarise the evidence you gave us just before the break? Of the three documents that are derived from the notes of the duty officer, the most contemporaneous is the duty officer's notebook; that's right, isn't it? Because it's notes that are literally written at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The duty officer's logbook or diary is effectively a summary of the duty officer's notebook; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the war diary is a summary of the notebook and other documentation within the command written up some days after the event?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you made reference when you were answering questions to Mr. Vanderpuye, to the report, the combat reports, that are issued by brigade command on a daily basis. There are basically two kinds, aren't there? There is a daily combat report and an interim combat report.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were regular daily reports and interim reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And would you mind telling us just a little bit about how the regular or daily reports came into existence and how many of them were issued on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, regular combat reports were to be issued twice a day. The command did one of them, and as required the command also made an interim report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was an interim report necessarily issued on a daily basis or was it only issued if it was justified by the circumstances within the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Interim combat reports were made only if that was necessary for extraordinary reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, I referred you earlier to the rules of the JNA about the duty officer and the duty officer's roster. But in fact, in the Zvornik Brigade, you wrote your own rules about the keeping of records and the creation of reports, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a note in the duty officer's room containing all the regulations, and they were adjusted regulations taken over from the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask you to look at two sections of the rules and I'm going to ask you to read them out because these haven't yet been translated. They'll appear on the computer screen in front of you in a little while and it is 65 ter number 7D442. And I'd like the witness first to be shown page 7. Are these the rules that you were just referring to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you would also have to show me the beginning. This begins with chapter 3, "Organisation of operations duty". Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Somebody to my left had just made exactly the same suggestion, that I should show you the first page. Do you still need to see the first page or can you identify it from what's in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be best if we show him page 1 then, just to be clear?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you show the first page it will be clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: There you are.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's a document from the operations organ of our command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Is it the case that you yourself wrote or adapted these rules for the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say definitely that it was me but it was the section that I headed. This is a format from 1993 that we didn't need to change. Maybe we added certain things but nothing major.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Then can we go back to page 7 and I'd like you, if you would, to read out to us point 11 that you were just looking at, the heading and then point 11.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was page 5, chapter 3, "Organisation of operations duty service"; is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Dragutinovic. And would you read out for us point 11?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Chief of Staff shall with his own order stipulate which officers are going to serve as operations duty officers." Do you want me to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No. Thank you. That's perfectly fine for my purposes but I'd like you now please to look at page 10. No, I'm sorry, page 8. And if the page can be brought down a little further, can you start to read point 14, which will go over the page? So can you read the first line and then we will go over the page to page 9.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Operations duty officers submit to the superior duty officer daily and interim reports, daily reports are submitted twice, once describing situation as of 1400 hours, the other one describing the situation as of 1800 hours. The first one has to be submitted by 1500 hours, the second one by 1900 hours. Interim reports are submitted as required," as I said a moment ago. We at the command submitted one daily report and if it became necessary we submitted two, but we did not have strict orders to submit two, although these instructions stipulate that we should submit two.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I'd just like you lastly to look at page 10, if you would, and I'll ask you some questions about that when it appears. I don't want to you read this out loud but this is an instruction as to the proper format for a daily combat report within the brigade, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And we'll probably find as we look at daily combat reports that each of the paragraphs in the report correspond to those numbers, and, for example, at number 7, at number 7, I think, it requires the duty officer always to report on a daily basis about losses within the brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Dragutinovic. I'm going to move on now to ask you a few questions about your boss, Mr. Obrenovic. Were you aware that he had first arrived in Zvornik with the JNA in February 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in Zvornik then but I know he was with the JNA unit in Zvornik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And were you also aware that at the time of the outbreak of war in Bosnia, Dragan Obrenovic was a member of the War Presidency in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: At the time of the outbreak of war in Zvornik, you were a member of the JNA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a member of the war unit of the JNA, but not in Zvornik, in Bijeljina rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that's my mistake but I wanted to establish that to ask you this question: Would it have been proper or permissible for a soldier contracted to the JNA to concurrently draw a salary or expenses as a member of a TO of a Serbian municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, no. Not during the existence of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to come to the outbreak of war in Bosnia. At the start of the war in a municipality such as Zvornik, all able-bodied men were mobilised, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Able-bodied men were mobilised into various units. Some into wartime units of the JNA. Others into units of Territorial Defence. And yet others were mobilised into units of civilian defence. And some were mobilised into the reserve forces of the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And even some may have been mobilised, I think, into working detachments?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the decision as to which of those units they would be mobilised to was dependent upon their experience and situation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It mostly depended on their military specialty as recorded in the register kept by the Ministry of Defence. That was a rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. You've answered my next question. When the Zvornik Brigade was formed, its personnel was derived from really six categories of soldiers. I want to see if you agree with this. The first category was professional soldiers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since I wasn't there when the Zvornik Brigade was established -- I know, in fact, that there were no professional soldiers in the Zvornik Brigade, although I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's my mistake again. The phrase I should have used was professional officers. There were some professional officers in the Zvornik Brigade when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And there were reserve officers?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, the command consisted of reserve officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the third category of officer would have been promoted officers?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not get that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You didn't hear it or you didn't understand what I was suggesting to you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand what you meant. What does "promoted officers" mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: People who became officers because of their experience within the unit.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I understand now. Many were promoted into officers on the basis of some criteria that were applied at the time, such as experience, and some sort of imposed themselves and received a rank, I don't know for what reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In terms of the other personnel, there were three categories: Reservists, recruits and soldiers under contract. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the beginnings of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I want you to talk from your own experience, the categories of soldier that you observed from the moment you were involved in it and throughout the time that you were an officer there.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I joined the Zvornik Brigade, there were some active duty officers, there were some reserve officers, and as for the troops, there were exclusively men from reserve forces. A very small number were conscripts, and there were no contract soldiers. I don't remember quite clearly but I know for sure that that category did not exist in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Would you agree that the substantial majority of the personnel of the Zvornik Brigade was made up of men who had been mobilised into TO units?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly, yes. Only some of them had been mobilised before that into wartime units of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, as to the command initially of the Zvornik Brigade, it's right, isn't it, that between May and December of 1992, the Zvornik Brigade had no fewer than five commanders?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The last of those was Vinko Pandurevic, but before him was a man called Major Dragan Petkovic who was wounded in 1992 and never thereafter commanded the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And so between October and December of 1992, the Zvornik Brigade had no commander at all?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That too is correct. After Major Petkovic, who was the commander then, was wounded, the brigade command had also lost some part of the territory they used to hold, and it practically fell apart. There was no commander, no Chief of Staff. Most of the organs of the command were missing. Only a small part remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: On the 1st of December, Dragan Obrenovic arrived as Chief of Staff of the Zvornik Brigade. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And a little while after that, on the 18th of December, Vinko Pandurevic arrived as commander of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: There was no ceremony when Vinko Pandurevic arrived to command the brigade, was there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I personally returned from one mission to the command that had been moved from my usual base in Karakaj, in Orahovac village, and there was an office that we ourselves designated as the commander's office, and there I found, upon my return, Commander Pandurevic, without knowing, prior to that, that he was there. But there was no ceremony, not that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And it's right, isn't it, that upon his arrival, he was briefed as to the situation within the brigade by the Chief of Staff, Dragan Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Were you present when this happened or have you -- were you informed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was only informed about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But in any event any briefing of the new commander about the situation of the brigade was pretty bleak, wasn't it? The situation in the brigade was close to disastrous.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Am I supposed to answer that? It was more than disastrous.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: To shorten matters, I'll put a couple of facts to you. The 2nd Battalion at that time was surrounded in the Drinjaca, do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The 6th Battalion had basically fallen apart after the massacre at Glodjansko Brdo?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It had fallen apart and stopped existing as a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the Lokanj Battalion had virtually collapsed as well; is that true?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Lokanj Battalion had a local commander. It was a local unit. And this commander had practically no contacts with the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've dealt briefly with the situation concerning the turnover of commanders of the brigade. Was the situation similar within the subordinate units of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was similar. All the units subordinated to the command had been established as local units, as -- with their local commanders, and the situation in those units was equally bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what sort of allegiance did the battalions have to brigade command at the time Vinko Pandurevic arrived in December of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please rephrase your question? It's very hard for me to understand what you mean by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. It's correct, isn't it, that most of the brigades were commanded in a way that showed no cohesion with brigade command? They behaved on an individual basis.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes. All the battalions were independent, and it was very difficult to control and command such units. No commander before could do that. Major Petkovic did make some attempts at that but his predecessors didn't do even that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to move on slightly to the size and definition of the Zvornik Brigade. The Zvornik Brigade was defined as a light infantry brigade, that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I want you now just to briefly consider a document, which is P382, so that we can see the numerical strength of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's a covering letter. We'll need to go forward a page or two maybe. It's really the figure at the bottom that I'm interested in the witness looking at. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, as operations officer, you were aware, weren't you, that the brigade had a numerical strength in excess of 5.000 men?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Just as it is indicated in this document. This document was produced by our organs, the assistant Chief of Staff for organisation and mobilisation and from my operations department. So this document does originate from our command and it does speak about the numerical strength.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: 5.000 men is a much larger unit than a light infantry brigade, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
