utterances.text: Yes. This is not a light infantry brigade. It would be more of an infantry brigade, but maybe the strength surpasses even that kind of formation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just think that we should indicate for the record the date of the document. I don't think that's been done. To put the testimony in context.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, we can go back to the first page and see the date of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The document speaks for itself. It says for the month of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, the fact that the Zvornik Brigade was defined as a light infantry brigade meant that it was given a command structure designed to suit a light infantry brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but let me just say that the number was the same in 1993. The figure might have differed slightly but the situation didn't change that much up to 1995. The structure was not the same but the number remained the same up to 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't know whether you considered my last question. I'll put it to you again, which is that the fact that the Zvornik Brigade was defined as a light infantry brigade meant that it was given a command structure that was designed to suit a light infantry brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Whereas in fact in terms of numerical strength, it was more like the size of a motorised brigade or even two light infantry brigades; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did that mean that effective control of the brigade's resources, with an understrength command structure, was very difficult?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was exactly the case. This structure of the brigade, and this structure of the command, called for everyday presence in the units. No day would pass when one or more officers were present in one or several battalions at the time. They had to be there every day in order to provide for the proper functioning of the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And in terms of the manpower, a particular problem was the conscripts who were permitted to work, as it were, half the time and be soldiers half the time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to correct you here. Not conscripts but members of the brigade units. They would spend some time in the brigade and they would stay at home after that. They would be providing for their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And was that done frequently in 10-day shifts so 10 days at home, 10 days on duty?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a shift warfare. Our commander used to say that we had weekend warriors. He meant it more as a joke but it did reflect the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And during the periods that the brigade members were at home or at work, they were outside the control or command of the unit. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were absolutely outside the control of the brigade command and their units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And of their very nature, the sort of members of the brigade who were farmers and workers and involved in activities within the Zvornik community were difficult by their very nature to command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in a brigade organised in this way, where a soldier spends only some time in the brigade under some sort of control, of course it was very hard to control them. We tried to introduce certain ways of controlling them outside their units. However, this failed and eventually we gave up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've already told us that in December of 1992, Vinko Pandurevic and Dragan Obrenovic arrived at the brigade to become commander and Chief of Staff respectively, and I want just now to explore with you how they were reacted to by the local community. It's right, isn't it, that they were both very young men when they arrived in 1992, in December?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Extremely young to hold the offices they had been given; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the perspective of the brigade as it was at the time, their respective ages did not provide any guarantees that they will be able to command the brigade. I myself was not bothered by their age.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Neither man was from Zvornik originally. That's true as well, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. They did not hail from Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And both of them were trained professional soldiers who wished to run the Zvornik Brigade along military lines?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were both officers trained in the former JNA. They had a lot of skill and knowledge about unit command, which obviously made them suitable to command the unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, if you don't mind, can I interrupt a minute?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Absolutely, Judge Kwon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Dragutinovic, it's about the weekend soldier, as you put it. You said that while they are off duty, they are absolutely outside the control of the brigade, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If that weekend soldier, while he's off duty, committed a crime, for example, a theft or killing, whatever, is he subject to the investigation by the civilian police or military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the time when they were not in the brigade, if something like that happened, the investigation would be carried out by the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Kwon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: From your observation of Dragan Obrenovic and Vinko Pandurevic, they were both men who took very seriously the orders they received from higher command, the Main Staff of the VRS and the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Picking up from the question of Judge Kwon and the witness's answer, granted that in such a case the investigation would be carried out by the civilian police, would it be correct to state that the military authorities, that's the Zvornik Brigade in this instance, even once an investigation has been carried out by the civilian police, would be entitled to ask the civilian police to transfer the person into the jurisdiction of the military courts of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If it was established that they were members of any of the VRS units, a request was made for their transfer, and they could be tried pursuant to the laws that applied to the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think I better join this party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're more than welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The modal verb you used was "could". I want you to imagine now, for example, that whilst on his 10 days of rest, a weekend soldier of the Zvornik Brigade committed a rape of a local woman and was arrested by the civilian police. Would it be the case that he had to be transferred to the authority of the military police or would the civilian police, on pursuit of her complaint, have seen through his prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question for me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. It's certainly not directed to me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought that maybe you were engaged in a debate on that. I'm sorry. If a soldier wearing civilian clothes had committed a crime which fell under the authority of the civilian police, the crime would be investigated by the civilian police. If the military investigating organs believed, and I'm just talking as far as I know about these things, that the soldier had committed a crime that might threaten the interests of the army of Republika Srpska, then a request would have been made for his transfer under the authority of the military organs. But I'm afraid you should ask that question the judges of the military courts and the legal experts who were better versed in such matters. I was just an army operative and I wouldn't be able to answer your question properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, thank you for trying any way. If you don't mind, because of the questions you were asked by the Judges and myself, I want to just recap where we were going. You've agreed with me that Vinko Pandurevic and Dragan Obrenovic were young officers who weren't from Zvornik, who were professional soldiers who took seriously the orders of the Main Staff and the Drina Corps. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the orders that they did receive from the Main Staff and the Drina Corps from time to time included them being required to commit Zvornik Brigade forces to other theatres of war in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were such orders, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And again, to recap some earlier questions, you've agreed with me that the Zvornik Brigade was mostly comprised of mobilised conscripts, these were people who were farmers, workers and family men, and soldiers I think only half of the time, and the units were accordingly difficult to command. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's how it was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And was it the case that the conscripts of the Zvornik Brigade were able to find a voice through the organs of the local community?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I am afraid I don't understand your question completely. Could you please rephrase it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. I'll put it this way: Men who were weekend soldiers in Zvornik were not particularly keen to be sent to fight in other areas of Bosnia, were they?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already stated that all the units were locally oriented. Everybody was very much interested in defending their own village. They were very closely tied to their own villages. And that's why the brigade was more of a local unit. It was very difficult to move it. It was not a manoeuvre unit, as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And equally, is it right that the organs of the local community were keen to keep the men local?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The political organs and the organs of local communities were also very much locally geared and that -- they found it very difficult to accept the commanders who came from outside. They wanted commanders to be their own, locals, and if possible, that they shared the same ideologies and political views.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree that neither the local community nor the conscripts themselves had much enthusiasm for a brigade organised along military lines?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very difficult to say that the brigade resembled a homogenous unit at the time. It would be very far-fetched to say that. It was very heterogenous. It was not easy to command. Everybody wanted to be a local commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you've led me to this question: In terms of professionalism, organisation and effectiveness, the Zvornik Brigade was completely different from the brigade as envisaged by the rules of the JNA, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was entirely different.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But that was what Vinko Pandurevic and Dragan Obrenovic were keen to achieve; you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with that. Only through their huge effort some results could be seen already in the early days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, the commander in particular did not allow community authorities to interfere with the command of the brigade, is that true?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true. And as a result, some problems arose. Local politicians wanted to interfere with the work of the command. They even wanted to command the units of the Zvornik Brigade, and the commander and the Chief of Staff absolutely didn't allow that to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I want to just look at a couple of examples of attempts to interfere in brigade command by local politicians, and to that end could we please look at 7D460, which has already been shown to a witness. It's a letter from Commander Pandurevic to corps command dated the 23rd of February 1993. Now, I'm not going to ask to you read all this out as Mr. Sarapa did with somebody else a couple of weeks ago but if you could just read through this letter and remind yourself of the incident that it is about, I've got a question to put to you. And please feel free to ask the usher to scroll the document down as you need to.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you show the top, please? No, sorry, scroll down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. Bourgon is present in the courtroom now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I see the bottom now, if there is any more? Okay. Well, basically this is clear enough. I knew about this document and I knew about the things it describes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we were talking a little while earlier about the immediate prior commander to Vinko Pandurevic, Major Petkovic. Do you recall an incident in February of 1993 when Vinko Pandurevic was away from the brigade command, when an attempt was made by local community members to replace him with his predecessor, Major Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And had they, in order to achieve that, enlisted the assistance of the Drina Corps commander, General Milenko Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that the corps commander was also involved in all these games, if I can say so, to replace Commander Pandurevic. I don't know for what reasons but they were certainly -- they had certainly nothing to do with military interests. This document reflects very precisely the situation and the commander wanted it all cleared up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I just want you to look quickly at another document which is 7D452, which is an order dated the 19th of April 1993. And if you don't mind, Mr. Dragutinovic, because this document hasn't been read into the record, I wonder if you could briefly read through this order for us.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you just scroll it down so I can see the commander's signature, it's Dragan Petkovic, as I thought. It says, "Temporary transfer of soldier Relja Petkovic, order."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness read more slowly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "With a view to organising spring sowing in Zelinje village, temporarily relieve Relja Petkovic from the 7th Battalion and return him to the command of Zelinje Company. The said soldier will be engaged in agricultural works without any remuneration, using the tractor from the company Zelinje command. The commander of Zelinje Company will relieve the said soldier of duty and issue him with a tractor from the company command and he will find him a replacement for -- from the reserve force of the company that is in Zelinje. Fuel for these works will be provided by every household head. This order to be executed by 1200 hours on the 20th April 1993. The person responsible for the execution of this order is the commander of the 7th Battalion."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. So in summary this is an order transferring a soldier from one unit to another; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to do some agricultural work, and it's not Pandurevic who signed this, it's Dragan Petkovic, who did this. I don't know how. I don't know who appointed him or who authorised him to perform the duties of the commander at the time when Pandurevic was the commander, and Pandurevic was not replaced at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just to be absolutely clear. Let us suppose even that Pandurevic was absent; the order could have been signed or should have been signed by Dragan Obrenovic, that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it should have been signed by the commander's deputy, unless a new commander is appointed in the absence of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Or just to deal with all the possibilities, the order could have borne the commander's name but have been signed on his behalf by some other officer?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If Pandurevic was the brigade commander, then this order should have been signed "Pandurevic" in typewritten text, and the signature, whoever signed for him, should specify, "For Commander Pandurevic."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just to be clear, in April of 1993, Dragan Petkovic had no authority whatsoever to issue orders as brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan Petkovic could only sign for the commander if somebody had appointed him to stand in for the commander temporarily, if the commander was absent for any reason. But in any case, it should have been Chief of Staff. I can't remember. I don't know why Dragan Petkovic was there at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you don't mind, you told us before that Petkovic was the Zvornik Brigade commander before Pandurevic, and that he was wounded, and that basically brought to an end his command and he was later replaced by General Pandurevic. Now, after he lost his command because of his injuries, did he remain in the Zvornik Brigade? Or did he leave the Zvornik Brigade completely? Did he continue to form part of the Zvornik Brigade, in other words, not as a commander but as a component of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was no longer a member of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So in relation to this document that Mr. Haynes has referred you to, what would be the -- his source of authority at the time, if you have knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't tell you that. Generally speaking about this document, I don't know how he came to be in the command post of the brigade or who gave him authorisation, if he had any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But to make it even more typical, the soldier named in this document is a close relative of his.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That explains a few things. Yes, Mr. Haynes. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just to finish off this topic, throughout the period that he was commander of the Zvornik Brigade, was Vinko Pandurevic a popular figure with local community institutions or politicians?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was certainly not popular with the politicians or anyone in the political leadership in Zvornik municipality. His rating with them was not very good, for all sorts of reasons, but mainly because he didn't let them interfere in the command over the Zvornik Brigade, something that they had kept trying to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dragutinovic. I'm now going to move on to an entirely different topic, which is the zones for which the Zvornik Brigade was responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I'm going to start by asking that P1463 be put into e-court, please. Now, initially I'm going to ask that we move to the bottom right-hand corner and blow the map up enough times for the witness to see his own signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Perhaps just a little more to the right.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see it. It's enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I wonder whether you'd be good enough just to identify your own signature on this map.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And can you just tell us a little bit about what this map in general shows?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the working map of the operations section. There are operations of the brigade drawn on this map, all the operations involving the Zvornik Brigade in 1995. Here below I see the combat operation Krivaja 95, and I suppose in other sections of the map there are similar indications of various operations including the dates so that the operations organ can follow the activities of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, so that we understand some of the things we are going to look at and forgive me I have to do it this way, I'm going to ask that we go and look at the legend in the bottom right-hand corner, I think. Yes, thank you. We have it there and just move across a little to the right. Thank you. Now, Mr. Dragutinovic, in preparing this map, actually I haven't asked you that. Did you draw this map? Or draw the marks upon it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made the map, and Major Galic with me. For the most part, the entries are mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You've made a legend in this section of the map, which we will see in greater detail in a minute.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm just interested that you tell us what, for example, the pink line means that is the very first entry on the legend.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Positions of the Zvornik Brigade on the 1st September 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And a similar shaded line in blue, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the enemy, the positions, the lines the enemy had reached, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm now going to show you this map in a different form. We have tried blowing it up on the computer but it simply disintegrates so we've had it blown up manually and I think we will have to show the witness and put it on the ELMO, please. For anybody who wants to move the map around on their own e-court, it's the central section of the map which centres on Zvornik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dragutinovic, can you help us here? The section of the map that you now see, does that effectively show the confrontation lines between the various battalions of the Zvornik Brigade and the forces of the 2nd Corps of the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's easier to see it here on the other side. This map shows 16th of July, the passage of the 28th Division, and the routes of its movement on the 16th of July in the defence area of the 4th Battalion, as well as other units that are to the left and to the right of this section of combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the positions of the battalion as shown on this map, are they accurate as at July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just see a moment. Yes. That's the situation as of July 1995. 7th, 4th, 6th, and 2nd Battalion, and further up are the 5th and the -- no, the 5th and the 1st are not actually shown, not in their entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In relation to each of the battalions, just so that we are clear, it's probably good if you stay where you are. We are looking there at the 4th Battalion. There appears to be drawn on the map a thin red line drawn in a sort of loop. What does that represent? Do you understand what I'm referring you to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 4th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. We could take any other battalion you want, if you want. Let's try the 3rd Battalion. Move the map slightly --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's take the 6th Battalion. It's the best visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It might be my mistake. I might have been looking at the 6th Battalion anyway. It's the loop that's in the middle of the page, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can take either the 6th or the 3rd. You just tell me what I'm supposed to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I want you to explain what is represented by the thin red line that comes back from the defence line --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the curved line? It shows the area of defence of that battalion. Let's take for instance the 6th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. If the witness could be offered a pointer and indicate the relevant parts so that we can follow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 6th Battalion. These are its basic positions. There were minor shifts. This was a prior position. After that it moved forward, took up some new positions. This is its area of defence, in Vjenacac area, there were reserve positions, back-up positions, of that battalion that were never occupied but they had been prepared. And here in the front part, there were fortified, prepared positions, and that's where the unit was positioned facing the other side. The same goes for the 3rd Battalion. Back-up positions are around Klisa, whereas basic positions are here. We see the command post of the 6th Battalion. It says Donja Baljkovica. In the area of 6th Battalion, we have the forward command post of the corps command. Anyway, these are areas of defence, where we see the 6th Battalion, 4th Battalion, and less visibly, the 7th Battalion. But the back-up positions of the 7th Battalion only go up to Cetino Brdo. These positions were prepared but never occupied. Back-up positions of the 3rd Battalion were in the area of Klisa, also prepared but not occupied. Then you see the positions of a various battalions, firing groups, Motovo for the 4th Battalion, Staro Selo for the 7th Battalion. That's the combat dispositions of the battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just to clarify something that you said earlier, the blue lines which are opposite the red lines are the lines of the enemy?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Those positions were held by units of the 2nd Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This entire section.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And we see two arrows there going through the area of defence of the 4th Battalion. What do they represent?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the 4th Battalion, they represent routes of passage and the agreed passage of the 28th Division, and here behind are the routes along which they came behind the lines of the 4th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dragutinovic. And if that is convenient to everybody that would be a convenient moment to take the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. There was a reference in the record to the corps command being situated in the vicinity of the 6th Battalion. I think that might have either been a translation error or certainly something that needs to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The forward command post of the brigade, not the corps. The forward command post of the brigade in Delici village, and the broader area of Kitovnice, that's what I'm showing now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's clear for us. We'll have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Dragutinovic, before we broke, you were illustrating on the blown-up map that you have by your side the areas of defence of the battalions of the Zvornik Brigade. I wonder if you would briefly describe your understanding of how the area of defence is defined for a battalion.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are, in fact, areas of defence for a battalion, whereas a brigade would have a zone of defence. The area of defence of battalions is defined by the disposition of units within that area; the basic position and the back-up position. I indicated the basic position of one of the battalions, that's the position facing the enemy, and the back-up position further in depth that we prepared and fortified but did not occupy. There are also other elements of defence: Firing group, command post, logistics or the rear, and all the other components of the battalion. It is defined and once the battalion is in the field, the battalion knows exactly what its area of defence is. In this case, on this working map, we can see it more clearly on the example of the 6th and the 3rd Battalion. We see their main disposition, in Boskovici and Pecine, the back-up position in Klisa, and the mixed artillery battalion was also there, but it didn't interfere with the area of defence. You see also all the other components of defence. On this map, you see the same elements for the 3rd Battalion, the basic positions and the back-up positions. The situation is similar with all the other battalions. Because this here is a working map that was drawn from 1993 onwards showing actions and activities of our brigade. In some places we moved forward, then retreated under enemy attack. It's a working map that shows movements over a longer period of time, movements of our units and also enemy units. In any case, you can see clearly what the area of defence of a certain battalion is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What is the principal difference between an area of defence and a zone of defence?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Areas of defence apply to tactical units, battalion and lower, whereas zones of defence apply to brigades. So the brigade has its own zone of defence, the left one and the right one, but it's not defined. It's only defined by the disposition of units. Wherever the units of the brigade are, with their respective tasks is the zone of defence of the brigade, if it's involved in defence. Anything outside the combat disposition of brigade units is not within the zone of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the brigade have any other zones which might come into play? For example, if it is in offensive operations?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brigade has its area of operations and axes of operation. But as for areas of responsibility, there is only such a thing as area of intelligence responsibility, namely the area in which intelligence units collect intelligence. Other zones, such as zones of fire, zones of artillery fire, zones of action of mechanised or artillery units and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd just like you now to look at another document, which is 7D441. This is a document from the Drina Corps command, which sets out, doesn't it, the zones of responsibility for combat activities of the various brigades subordinate to the Drina Corps command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Have you seen it before?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall. I probably saw it before, because it's from 1992. It originated in the Drina Corps. I expect your question will have to do with the zones of responsibility of brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'd just like you to familiarise yourself with paragraph 1A which sets out the zone of responsibility --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what I'm going to do is ask you firstly whether all those areas are familiar to you.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And then I'm going to show you another plan, which is P02109, which is a pictorial depiction of the area described for the Zvornik Brigade. And I'd be obliged if we could blow this map up just to focus on the area which has on the -- has on it the 1st Zvornik Infantry Brigade. This map, which we've seen in this case, has a red line depicting what is said to be the Drina Corps area of responsibility. And it's the red line. The black line you should recognise is the confrontation line between you and the Muslim forces, both for your brigade and others. And do you acknowledge that the document you've just read depicting the Zvornik Brigade's zones of responsibility for combat activity is depicted by the red line around the area next to the 1st Zvornik Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I want to take this very carefully. Do you still have the plastic-coated blown-up working map on the ELMO to your right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: If you look very carefully on that map, you should see that the red line on the plan we've got on e-court is actually on that map as well. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But it's quite faint. What I'm going to ask you to do is to -- I'm going to ask to you reinforce that line with a pen, please. Probably black would be the best colour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Where do you want him to reinforce that line? On the document which is on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: On the document which is on the ELMO, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can it be done?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, we've got a permanent marker pen and the map can then become an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead. I can't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Dragutinovic, would you please, as it were, reinforce the thin red line that's on that map by drawing over it with the black pen that you now have, to indicate where that line falls on the map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Basically Mr. Haynes is asking to you write over the red line with the black pen that you have been given. Retrace the red line, in other words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And I think we need you to put your initials somewhere along that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, he hasn't quite finished yet because the line goes further to the left, to the edge of the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I wonder if you would be good enough to finish off the line by going further to the left to the edge of the map?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I think if the map is pulled slightly up there is a further section of the red line which comes again out of the left-hand side of the map, across and down.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And now, if you be so good, can you put your initials on it and date the 14th of June 2007?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, thank you very much, Mr. Dragutinovic. You can see from the more simplistic version of the plan on the computer screen before you, that the area of responsibility for combat activities as defined by the document you looked at includes an area which, on the map and on the plan, is behind enemy lines, so far as you're concerned. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear. You can see it on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was that an area which, during the period you were in the Zvornik Brigade you ever had any control over or responsibility for?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this part of the territory, there was no contact, apart from contact with the enemy at the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: During the course of the war, it's right, isn't it, that the organs of state and community continued to function? There was local government, people went to school, there were civilian police forces and the like?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: As operations officer, did you ever consider the brigade to have any authority over public or private facilities that were outside your zones of defence?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brigade has jurisdiction only in the zone of defence and within the combat disposition of its units, and on -- and in buildings that were requisitioned for purposes of the Zvornik Brigade. Everything else was under the authority of local civilian authority. Because life went on. Schools were open, businesses were open, the parliament sat, the police operated, local communes. I don't think two different authorities can function in one and the same place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just a couple of other things on this issue. Until the 29th of July of 1995, it's correct that no state of war was declared in Republika Srpska, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. There was no state of war until the -- until 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And lastly this: The Zvornik Brigade was named the Zvornik Brigade because the people who made up its numbers came from Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exclusively from Zvornik municipality. And also some refugees who had moved into Zvornik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It wasn't named the Zvornik Brigade to indicate that it had a responsibility for every public and private building or facility within the municipality of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units of the VRS were not depicted by numbers. They were given names according to the place from which most of the soldiers were recruited. It has nothing to do with the territory or their responsibility for that territory, because they were responsible only for the combat disposition of their units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed. Now, I'm going to move on to another topic. You are familiar with the actions of the 8th Operational Group and the 28th Division of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And it's correct that on the 6th of November of 1992, at Glodjansko Brdo, the 8th Operational Group inflicted very substantial losses on the forces of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that offensive included the losses not only of soldiers but of civilians?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In that area there were also civilian population areas, and some civilians were killed along with the troops who were in Glodjansko Brdo, Kamenica. That is the southern part of Zvornik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Would it be right to suggest that the losses suffered at Glodjansko Brdo were probably the greatest losses suffered in one day by the Zvornik Brigade in its whole history?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the greatest losses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, in early 1993, did you take part in an action that involved the liberation of Glodjansko Brdo by the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And when Glodjansko Brdo had been liberated, did you uncover evidence of atrocities, torture and mass graves of Serbian soldiers and civilians?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there, but a commission was established, including UN forces, medical experts, pathologists, police experts, army experts, and they did the excavations, the exhumations, and determined the manner in which both soldiers and civilians were executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to have a look at some brief passages of television footage and see whether they are familiar to you from what you saw at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: For those who want to follow this in the English, there is a surrogate sheet it's 7D626 which translates the dialogue that we hear into English. And can we play now, please, the three sections of video, that's 5.39 to 6.25, 7.40 to 8.30, and 9.20 to 9.04 [sic], I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were those images similar to what you saw when you took part in the operation at Glodjansko Brdo or saw on your television shortly afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This footage is related to those events. That much I could see. And I've said already that I wasn't there for the exhumation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you recall there being a large funeral at Standard barracks which was attended by President Karadzic and his Minister of Defence, at which I think something like 38 soldiers from the Zvornik Brigade were buried?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was at the local cemetery, close to the barracks. That's where the soldiers were buried. Karadzic and his close associates were also present.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, in March of 1993, did you take part in an operation against the 8th Operative Group from Srebrenica as part of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I participated also as the operative officer of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And were those -- was that offensive eventually brought to an end by an order from President Karadzic, after Srebrenica had been declared a safe area by General Morillon?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime before our offensive was launched on the 19th of January or maybe the 17th of January, in which the Zvornik Brigade itself participated there was a series of events that I need to mention at this point: Those were attacks by the 28th Division and the operative group from the direction of Srebrenica against our positions on the village of Kravica and all the neighbouring villages that they took and torched. But let me put it this way: There was no intervention on the part of the media or the United Nations, for that matter. After that, our offensive was launched. On the 15th of March we managed to regain Kravica. We encircled Srebrenica and we destroyed parts of the 28th Division and that operations group, and finally when there was a showdown, President Karadzic ordered all the operations to be stopped, and General Morillon eventually entered Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, after that, you were aware, were you, that the United Nations was supplying the enclave of Srebrenica by convoys of lorries?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of that. Most of those convoys passed through the Karakaj pass where the command of the Zvornik Brigade was as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I want you just very briefly to explain, if you would, how it was that the convoys of lorries were licensed to pass through Karakaj and on to Srebrenica. What was the system of notification to you as to what was on the lorries or what was supposed to be on the lorries?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the command of the Zvornik Brigade, pursuant to an order by the commander, and I suppose by -- pursuant to an order of the superior command, there was a liaison officer with the UNPROFOR. Every convoy was announced to the superior command, and the duty operations officer of the higher Supreme Command informed our duty operations officer and our liaison officer would go to the pass and met the convoys there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And in what form did the notification to you take? Did you receive a list or -- of what had been authorised to be transported?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was known exactly what the convoy had reported as carrying, and based on the notification of materiel, technical equipment and so on and so forth, the liaison officer, together with the officer in command of the convoy, agreed on the contents of the convoy. If there was something missing when the contents were collated with the list, the liaison officer reported that to the superior command and asked for further instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like you now to look just at another short section of video.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's the same video, V00064821A. Again, there is a surrogate sheet with a translation of the dialogue should anybody wish to follow it in English, and it's minutes 18.23 to 19.08, please. It's the same exhibit number as the last surrogate sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: If we let that run on - we are not going to - we would be able to see that that was a convoy that was stopped in Zvornik. Do you recall that convoy being stopped that contained, amongst other things, satellite telephones, stoves, tents, and the like?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember this particular case but I can remember another case. I wouldn't be able to give you the exact date but the case was rather similar to this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, by all means, in the case that you can recall, what was it that was found on the lorries that was not authorised to be transported by the lists?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion, a convoy was being checked and the contents collated with the list, and a lot of radio sets were found. That surpassed all the requirements of that particular unit. The unit was on the strength of the French Battalion and these radio sets were used and could be used only by military units. And as far as I can remember, they could not account for the presence of such a huge number of these radio sets and finally this radio equipment ended on our side. A compromise had been reached in contacts with the superior command, and finally they agreed to leave these radio sets in our brigade. However, we could not use them because they used special batteries that we ourselves could not find. We did not have them. We could not obtain them in any way. That is just one convoy that I remember. And the convoy itself was headed for Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in relation to the convoy that we saw on the video we just watched, according to the translation of what was being said there, what was found amongst the transported goods were tents, satellite communication devices, and stoves. You're an operations officer. It's pretty obvious what you could use a satellite communications device for, and a tent. What military use might stoves be put to within the enclave of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the stoves could be intended for the population. But if they were not on the lists that had been submitted to the superior commands for the approval of passage, then anything that was not on the list had to be accounted for, and as for the satellite devices and the rest of the things, I don't think any comment is necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, after the creation of the enclave of Srebrenica, you were aware, weren't you, that Muslim forces from within the enclave were carrying out combat activities in the villages surrounding Srebrenica by attacking Serbian villages and the like?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that because the units of the 28th Division had not been disarmed, and if this was a demilitarised zone there should not have been any active military units. And let me just say one more thing. When we entered Srebrenica, the part where the surrendered weapons were to be found, those weapons were only trophy weapons that could be held even by civilians, and so on and so forth. In other words the 28th Division functioned unhindered and carried out various attacks beyond the protected area, in the neighbourhoods and villages that leaned on the protected area. And it is also known that in 1995 that parts of the 28th Division were on the Sarajevo front line and there were some indications that some other parts of that unit would start moving towards Kladanj and Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were you aware that there was a regular corridor used between Srebrenica and Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And was that a corridor that was used in both directions?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would often happen that the same corridor was used for those going from Srebrenica towards Tuzla and vice versa. In part, that corridor was in the area controlled by the Zvornik Brigade, but there were no units deployed there, so that corridor was in use for quite some time. This is the Jajici-Pandurica-Crni Vrh-Kamenica-Udrc-Srebrenica sector that I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did the brigade take any steps to try and prevent the use of the corridor?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When units were deployed in that area, we managed to interrupt that sort of communication between the free territory under the control of the BiH army and units from Srebrenica. Later on, they moved that area to the left and to the right but we stepped up our control and we managed to reduce the movement along that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dragutinovic. Have a rest this afternoon. I'm finished for the day but I'll have some more questions for you tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Mr. Dragutinovic, we'll continue tomorrow. In the meantime, there is one rule that we need to observe, that is not to allow anyone to discuss with you or you try to discuss with anyone the subject matter of your testimony. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I am clear on that and I've already been told that before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So we stand adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9.00. One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, how much more time do you require, do you reckon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: During the last break, I had pause for thought, and if you haven't already received it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. I think I will be the whole of tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have not objected to much of this material that is beyond the scope, and frankly, repetitive. Some of it is not contested. And -- but three more hours beyond the estimate seems a bit much. So if we could at least maybe tomorrow morning, if we could get a bit better picture from counsel where he's going. As a Defence witness, if we can save sometime having him be a Defence witness now, we don't have a problem with that, but this is making it very hard for us to plan, and if we could find out if anybody else has -- wants to add another four hours on to their estimates, we would like to know that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll come to that tomorrow morning. At the same level, I mean, Mr. Vanderpuye, also indicated when I asked him the first time he said two hours and he's gone much beyond those two hours. So let's deal with it tomorrow morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
